en: The *Buddhadharmakāya-sūtra*,
translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmaśrī, Imperially Appointed Great Master of Illuminating Teaching, Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments,
Subject Faxian, under Imperial Decree during the Western Heaven (India).
At that time, the World-Honored One, amidst the great assembly, spoke these words with a subtle and wondrous voice:
"The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, possess two kinds of bodies, both of which are endowed with merits as numerous as the sands of the Ganges."
What are these two? They are the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) and the dharma body (*dharmakāya*).

As for the transformation body, it manifests as being born from parents, endowed with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics that adorn its form. With the eye of wisdom, it universally observes all sentient beings; when the wise gaze upon it, their hearts feel joy, and their three karmas become purified. Each mark and characteristic is complete with a hundred merits, and such adornments consist of hundreds of thousands of accumulations of merit. All these marks of a great man are subsumed within the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).

Furthermore, he is fully endowed with the ten powers (*daśabala*), the four fearlessnesses (*caturvaiśāradya*), the three unfailing dharmas (*trīṇy avivāryadharmāṇi*), the three foundations of mindfulness (*trīṇi smṛtyupasthānāni*), the three ways in which he needs no protection (*trīṇy arakṣyāṇi*), and the four immeasurables (*catvāry apramāṇāni*). He possesses each of the supreme Nārāyaṇa-strengths of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa*). Such, in brief, are the adorned virtues of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, which are complete and perfect; this is called the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body).
"Furthermore, the Dharma-body of all Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, is inconceivable and immeasurable, such that no one is able to proclaim it extensively."

Even if pratyekabuddhas and śrāvakas—such as Śāriputra and others, who possess the most superior faculties, are well-versed in the profound Dharma, and have attained great wisdom and clear penetration into various meanings—were unable to extensively proclaim the merits of the dharmakāya.

The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are the teachers of the three realms; as those of great compassion, they bring great benefit to all sentient beings, protecting and mindful of them with equanimity and without discrimination. Abiding in *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, they are further skilled in the three methods of subduing and well able to deliver others from the four difficulties. Possessing the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), they practice the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) throughout the long night. Free from the five desires, they transcend the suffering of the five destinies; they possess the six factors of the Dharma and fulfill the six *pāramitās*. They open the flowers of the seven factors of enlightenment and expound the eightfold noble path; they are skilled in understanding the nine kinds of *samāpatti* and possess the ten powers of knowledge (*jñānabala*).
By means of this power of wisdom, my fame is heard throughout the ten directions; therefore, I am called the Supreme Heavenly Being (*paramārthadeva*).

Throughout time, space, and location, three times by day and three times by night, I constantly observe that no one is able to extensively expound such internal qualities and dharmas of the Buddhas as I do. For this reason, I now briefly explain this Dharma.

"This Dharma-body is pure and singular, non-dual, untainted, and unconditioned; it should be cultivated and realized. All conditioned phenomena arise from the unconditioned. Such is the reality: it is without purity, without defilement, without thought, and without dependence. Transcending all expedient means, it serves as the great refuge for sentient beings. All dharmas practiced by sentient beings are free from faults; this is the truly wholesome dharma, free from all recollections. Within the boundless gates of samādhi, it is unmoving and unwavering, thereby attaining liberation."

By means of the two kinds of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, one attains liberation through the desire to be free from desire; one is liberated from the dharmas of ignorance and craving by means of wisdom; one understands the dharmas of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) through mindfulness; and through liberation by clear knowledge, one thoroughly penetrates their intrinsic nature. Thus, one is deeply able to maintain mindfulness toward all dharmas, skillfully generating the dharma of *āpatti* from *āpatti*, and skillfully generating the dharma of *samāpatti* from *samāpatti*, without seeking or realizing anything among all dharmas.

Apart from these two dharmas, there is no object of cognition and nothing further to be cultivated; yet, by means of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), one ultimately accomplishes the three dharmas of ultimate consummation, the three dharmas of the roots of goodness, and the three gates of skillful means. Free from all false conceptualizations, one attains true birth.
"One realizes three kinds of wisdom, namely: hearing, reflection, and cultivation.
One is free from three types of defilement, namely: afflictions, karma, and suffering.
There are three kinds of samādhi, namely: emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness."
They are also called the three gates of liberation, namely the gates of liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
There are also three aggregates of phenomena, namely the aggregates of ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
There are three kinds of training in the Dharma, namely the training in ethical discipline (*śīla*), meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*).

There are three kinds of cultivation, namely the cultivation of ethical discipline, the cultivation of meditative concentration, and the cultivation of wisdom; these pertain to those in training (*śaikṣa*), those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and those who are neither in training nor beyond training.
There are three kinds of paths, namely: the path of seeing, the path of cultivation, and the path of no-more-learning.
There are three kinds of faculties, namely: the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," the faculty of "knowing," and the faculty of "one who has known."
There are three types of practice: namely, the noble practice (*ārya-caryā*), the celestial practice (*deva-caryā*), and the Brahma practice (*brahma-caryā*).
There are three categories of discernment: namely, the aggregates (*skandha*), the sense bases (*āyatana*), and the elements (*dhātu*).
Having understood these three dharmas, one attains a great mass of merit, realizes liberation, and achieves the tranquil nirvana—the three non-empty foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
The Tathāgata equally protects all sentient beings; regarding the threefold aggregates of phenomena, there are three types of persons, namely: superior, middling, and inferior.
"The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, possess three kinds of great compassion: namely, great compassion without object, subtle and wondrous great compassion, and great compassion for all sentient beings."
There are three kinds of mastery: namely, mastery over the body, mastery over the world, and mastery over the Dharma.

There are three qualities of non-protection: namely, that the bodily karma of all Tathāgatas is pure and free from impurity; their verbal karma is pure and free from impurity; and their mental karma is pure and free from impurity.
There are three kinds of swords: namely, the sword of hearing, the sword of reflection, and the sword of cultivation.
There are three kinds of supreme states: namely, the supremacy of concentration, the supremacy of wisdom, and the supremacy of liberation.
There are three kinds of dharma-realms, namely: right abandonment, detachment from desire, and cessation.
Furthermore, there are three realms, namely: the realm of desire, the realm of form, and the formless realm.

There are three kinds of clear knowledges of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa-vidyā*): namely, the clear knowledge of past lives, the clear knowledge of the divine eye regarding the future, and the clear knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows in the present.
There are three kinds of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*): namely, the impermanence of all conditioned formations, the selflessness of all phenomena, and the tranquility of nirvāṇa.
There are three kinds of enlightenment: namely, the enlightenment of the śrāvaka, the enlightenment of the pratyekabuddha, and unsurpassed enlightenment.
There are three kinds of knowledge of those beyond training: namely, the knowledge of exhaustion, the knowledge of non-arising, and the knowledge of right view.
The Three Jewels, the three refuges, and the three supreme knowledges;
the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the four factors of confidence, and the four phrases of liberation.

“There are four kinds of wholesome dharmas: namely, the wholesome in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha-kuśala*), the wholesome by intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-kuśala*), the wholesome by origination (*samutthāna-kuśala*), and the wholesome by association (*saṃprayoga-kuśala*).
There are also the four dharmas to be cultivated, the four dharmas of knowledge, the four noble truths, the four dhyānas, and the four wheels of the treasury.”
There are four dharmas and four reliances, namely: associating with virtuous friends, hearing the true Dharma, reflecting with focused mindfulness, and practicing according to the principle.

Furthermore, there are four conditions, namely: the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), and the object condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).

The four stages of application (*prayoga-avasthā*) are the stage of warmth (*uṣmagata*), the stage of summits (*mūrdhan*), the stage of patience (*kṣānti*), and the stage of the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*).

There are four types of paths (*mārga*): the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*), the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*), the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), and the path of excellence (*viśeṣa-mārga*).
There are the four fruits of śrāmaṇya and the four noble lineages; there are the four immeasurable minds, namely loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.

Furthermore, there are the four modes of birth, the four noble abodes, the four foundations of mindfulness, and the four postures; there are the four doors of emergence, namely emerging, entering, tranquility, and perfect awakening.
Furthermore, there are four stages of realization:
the five aggregates of those in training (*śaikṣa*), the five bases of liberation, the five factors for successive births, and the five noble conceptualizations of wisdom.

There are five divisions of *samādhi*, namely: the division of right abandonment, the division of subduing, the division of freedom from faults, the division of freedom from signs, and the division of freedom from intrinsic nature.

Furthermore, there are five kinds of supreme factors (*agra-bhāga*), five modes of manifestation, the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), the five aggregates (*skandha*), the five elements (*dhātu*), as well as the five aggregates of clinging (*upādāna-skandha*), six qualities of merit (*guṇa-dharma*), the six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and the six recollections (*anusmṛti*).

Furthermore, there are six kinds of dharmas, five kinds of detachment from desire, six kinds of cultivated practices, six stages of the path of vision, six modes of continuous practice, and six perceptions of realization.

The seven types of persons (*pudgala*), the seven practices of a great man (*mahāpuruṣa*), the seven stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*), the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), the seven faultless qualities (*anavadyadharma*), the seven methods for enjoying the concentration (*samādhi*), the seven sublime qualities (*saddharma*), the seven divisions of the elements (*dhātubheda*), the seven bases of skillful understanding (*kuśalavibhāgasthāna*), and the sevenfold path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
The eightfold path, the eight types of *pudgala*, and the eightfold Prātimokṣa precepts;

furthermore, the eight liberations, the eight bases, the eight knowledges, the eight paths, the eight precepts, the eight assemblies, as well as the eight worldly dharmas—the Tathāgata’s continuity is true, eternal, diligent, pure, and unstained by attachment.

Furthermore, there are nine kinds of past *samāpattis*, nine factors of the mind of faith, nine factors of realization, nine cessations of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), nine abodes of sentient beings, nine kinds of bases for reliance, nine untainted stages (*anāsrava-bhūmi*), and nine stages of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).
There are ten types of *pudgalas*: namely, the four candidates for the fruits and the four who have attained them, the ninth being the *pratyekabuddha*, and the tenth being the *samyaksambuddha*.

There are also the ten universal wholesome mental factors (*mahābhūmika-kuśala-dharma*), the ten qualities of those in training (*śaikṣa-dharma*), the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the ten paths of wholesome action, the ten paths of unwholesome action, the ten noble abodes (*āryavihāra*), and the ten methods of acting in accordance with reality (*yoniśo-manasikāra*).

The eleven dharmas of recollecting the marks and signs of merit; the eleven kinds of dharmas for being fully endowed with the wisdom of skillful understanding; the eleven kinds of dharmas for being fully endowed with the precepts.
The twelve kinds of arising speech; the twelve bases; the twelve links of dependent origination; and the twelve moments for realizing the noble Dharma.
The thirteen factors of joy, the thirteen factors of arising, the thirteen stages of activity;
the fourteen types of transformative minds;
and the fifteen moments of mind in the path of vision.
The sixteen moments of right mindfulness;
the seventeen aspects of those in training (*śaikṣa*); the seventeen aspects of aspiration;
the eighteen elements (*dhātu*); and the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*).
Nineteen: the *vibhaṅga-bhūmi* (stages of analysis).
Twenty-two: the faculties (*indriya*).

Thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*), namely: the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), the five faculties (*indriya*), the five powers (*bala*), the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), and the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*).
The forty-four dharmas of knowledge, further the seventy-seven dharmas of knowledge, and the one hundred and sixty-two paths— these are called the stages of cultivation.

Such immeasurable and boundless dharmas of continuous, true, and eternal nature, which are free from all afflictions, profoundly deep, vast, subtle, and inconceivable, are understood by the Great Wise One as they truly are.

This Buddha-dharma is the sublime dharma of as many Perfectly Enlightened Ones (*samyaksambuddha*) as there are grains of sand in the Ganges; it is the dharma of equality. If there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, or followers of other paths such as the Nirgranthas who seek to realize the wisdom of perfect enlightenment, those possessing right knowledge understand it as it truly is and further proclaim it extensively for the sake of sentient beings. Just as the Buddha has manifested it, they cause immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) sentient beings to all fully realize the quiescent, fearless, ultimate nirvāṇa.
The Sūtra on the Dharma-body Spoken by the Buddha.
